description: We are working on NASA spaceapps
summary: When a crew loses contact with Earth, routine health checks still need to happen. Team Antares built AstroMed, an onboard health monitoring station that lets crew members record measurements, spot changes and decide what to recheck while medical support is out of reach. A crew member taps an RFID card to start a session. An Arduino and ESP32 send sensor readings over the local network, and an ultrasonic sensor counts push-ups and logs each completed set. A guided check-in adds information that crew members enter themselves. The dashboard combines these records with explainable risk flags and individual trends. If a reading warrants escalation, AstroMed can prepare a summary for the crew to share when communications return. The system runs on a local computer without an internet connection. We built and tested a working breadboard prototype that others can reproduce using our wiring guide. We verified the PCB design in simulation. A physical PCB has yet to be fabricated.
details:
The problem. A long-duration mission can keep crews out of immediate contact with Earth and with the medical teams that normally help interpret health changes. We wanted a tool that crew members could use during that gap to maintain a record, recognize when a reading warrants a recheck and prepare useful information for the next conversation with the ground.

From the crew member to the dashboard. A crew member taps an RFID card on an RC522 reader to associate a session with their record. An Arduino UNO reads a fingertip LED and photoresistor for pulse, a wrist thermistor for skin temperature and a DHT11 for cabin temperature and humidity. A tilt switch registers movement. The Arduino passes JSON to an ESP32 over serial. The ESP32 forwards timestamped messages over local Wi-Fi while the session is active, with routine telemetry sent every two seconds. An HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor counts repetitions during a ground-based push-up test. A completed set is recorded as a single event. The browser check-in lets crew members enter their mood and optionally record blood pressure and fasting glucose from separate measurements.

How the crew uses the result. A Python and FastAPI backend validates and stores messages in SQLite and streams updates to a browser console through WebSockets. The console uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript. A rules engine assigns levels from 0 to 3 and shows the measurements and rules that triggered a flag, along with suggested next steps. Missing readings remain visible as missing. When a trend has enough observations, the console plots the existing measurements alongside a linear estimate. The engine evaluates changes in push-up counts against the crew member’s own history. For flagged situations, the crew can copy a prepared summary for sharing with ground support.

What we built and what we tested. One local station combines sensor readings, exercise events and self-reported data in a single crew record. The ESP32 can queue messages and retry when the local connection drops. A simulator sends the same JSON messages so the team can exercise the backend and dashboard when the hardware is unavailable. We built and tested the sensor station on a breadboard. The working prototype can be reproduced with standard components using the published wiring guide and firmware. We also designed a custom PCB in KiCad to consolidate the wiring and verified that the design worked in simulation. Physical fabrication and testing of the PCB are still pending. We used NASA references to inform the cabin environment rules and the comparison with a personal exercise baseline. Push-up counts are a prototype proxy for exercise performance. The sensors and thresholds are intended for demonstration and would need validation before use in crew health operations.
